title: Factor Rotation Playground
summary: Twelve fictional adjective markers in a two-dimensional factor space. Students rotate the axes and watch every loading change while the configuration of points, each communality and the total variance explained stay exactly where they were — then meet a genuine cross-loading and a pair of clusters that no orthogonal rotation can fit.
learningObjectives: State precisely what rotation changes and what it leaves invariant.
Explain why rotation neither manufactures results nor identifies a uniquely true solution.
Distinguish orthogonal from oblique solutions and treat the choice as a substantive claim about the constructs.
Recognise a genuine cross-loading as information rather than a nuisance.
Defend simple structure as an adopted criterion rather than a discovery.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, select and buttons; rotation is driven by a slider rather than by dragging, so WCAG 2.5.7 is satisfied by construction. The loading plot is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table of every loading, communality and salience decision; markers are labelled by name on the plot itself and the two axes are distinguished by dash pattern as well as colour. Sliders announce meaningful values ('axes 55 degrees apart, oblique solution, factors correlate 0.57'). An invariants box states in words what has not changed after each rotation. Reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Factor analysis: what rotation changes, what it cannot change, and why simple structure is a criterion rather than a discovery
simulationNotes: Three fictional marker sets with coordinates chosen to make three situations legible: a clean two-cluster structure, one containing a genuine cross-loading, and one whose clusters sit about 55 degrees apart. No correlation matrix was factored and no real study is represented. Rotation is applied as a coordinate transform; oblique solutions read loadings against non-perpendicular axes and report the implied factor correlation as the cosine of the angle between them. Pattern and structure coefficients are not distinguished, the number of factors is fixed at two, and the 'find the simplest structure' control is a coarse sweep rather than varimax, oblimin or promax.
